content: MUL1, or Mitochondrial E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1, is an enzyme encoded by the MUL1 gene located on chromosome 1 in humans. This enzyme is specifically localized to the outer mitochondrial membrane, where it plays a critical role in regulating mitochondrial morphology and apoptosis through various signaling pathways, including Akt, JNK, and NF-κB. Its pro-apoptotic function implicates it in the pathogenesis of cancer and Parkinson’s disease. The MUL1 gene encodes one of the E3 ubiquitin ligases. The human MUL1 protein is approximately 40 kDa in size and consists of 352 amino acids. It contains RING domains at both its N-terminal and C-terminal regions, which are exposed to the cytosol. The C-terminal RING finger domain is homologous to those found in the IAP (inhibitor of apoptosis protein) family and is responsible for its E3 ligase activity. Additionally, MUL1 is predicted to have two mitochondrial transmembrane helices, with the first domain serving as the primary anchor for the rest of the exposed protein. Despite lacking a conserved N-terminal signal peptide or mitochondrial targeting sequence, its transmembrane domains influence its trafficking and insertion into the mitochondrial membrane. MUL1 exhibits weak E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase activity. E3 ubiquitin ligases function by accepting ubiquitin from an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme in the form of a thioester and subsequently transferring the ubiquitin to specific substrate proteins. MUL1 preferentially ubiquitinates AKT1 at lysine-284 through lysine-48-linked polyubiquitination, targeting phosphorylated AKT for proteasomal degradation and thereby regulating Akt signaling. It is also proposed to act as a SUMO E3 ligase under physiological conditions. MUL1 is anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane and plays a role in controlling mitochondrial morphology. It promotes mitochondrial fragmentation and influences mitochondrial localization, potentially through its ability to sumoylate DNM1L. MUL1 has been observed to shuttle between mitochondria and peroxisomes, where it may also regulate peroxisome fission. Additionally, it inhibits cell growth and, when overexpressed, activates JNK via MAP3K7/TAK1, inducing caspase-dependent apoptosis. MUL1 is involved in modulating innate immune defense against viruses by inhibiting DDX58-dependent antiviral responses. It can mediate DDX58 sumoylation, disrupt its polyubiquitination, and activate NF-κB to initiate mitochondria-to-nucleus signaling under stress. Clinically, MUL1 is significant due to its pro-apoptotic functions. Apoptosis, or programmed cell death, involves structural changes such as cell shrinkage, plasma membrane blebbing, nuclear condensation, and DNA fragmentation. These changes result in the formation of apoptotic bodies, which are rapidly cleared by phagocytes to prevent inflammation. Apoptosis is a highly regulated process that plays a vital role in embryonic development and the removal of unwanted cells during normal tissue homeostasis. MUL1 is highly expressed in most human tissues under normal conditions but is notably absent in cancer cells derived from the lung, liver, colon, and kidney. This suggests that MUL1 functions as a tumor suppressor and is downregulated in cancer cells. Experimental studies in Drosophila and mammalian systems have shown that MUL1 binds and ubiquitinates mitofusin, indirectly regulating the PINK1/parkin pathway. This ability allows MUL1 to rescue phenotypes observed in PINK1 or parkin knockout mice, which explains the subtle dopaminergic neuronal degeneration and mitochondrial morphology changes observed in these models. Consequently, MUL1 is a promising therapeutic target for treating Parkinson’s disease. MUL1 has also been implicated as a modulator of antiviral signaling. It interacts with mitochondrial antiviral signaling proteins and catalyzes post-translational modifications of RIG-I, inhibiting RIG-I-dependent cell signaling. Depletion of MUL1 enhances RIG-I-mediated NF-κB and interferon-β activity, boosting the antiviral response and increasing pro-inflammatory cytokines following exposure to RNA mimetics like poly I:C or Sendai virus. This suggests that MUL1 is a novel regulator of RIG-I-like receptor-dependent antiviral responses, functioning to limit inflammation. As a regulator of viral-induced interferon production and pro-inflammatory cytokine induction, MUL1 inhibits RIG-I-induced signaling and mediates the cell’s antiviral and inflammatory responses through mitochondrial antiviral signaling proteins. MUL1 is known to interact with several proteins, including itself (MUL1), DNM1L, TAK1, and mitofusin.
